articles.title: UK autumn forecast: El Niño to cause wetter and warmer-than-normal season
articles.summary: A warmer and wetter-than-normal autumn is in store for the UK, according to the latest Met Office forecasts.
articles.body:
The UK is set for wetter and warmer-than-normal weather this autumn, driven by a strengthening El Niño, according to the latest forecasts from the Met Office.

The climate phenomenon - forecast to be the strongest in living memory - will influence a change to stormier conditions later this season.

Potential wetter weather will put areas of the UK gripped by drought on the road to recovery, but it could also bring an increased chance of flooding as a result.

An already warming climate, paired with unusually high sea temperatures around the UK, will also contribute to above-average temperatures.

El Niño to increase chances of stormy weather

A stormy season is forecast for the UK with the chances of wet and windy weather higher than normal, particularly from November.

"The latest seasonal forecasts suggest an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions as we move through autumn, which would be consistent with the historical influence of El Niño events," Met Office Chief Meteorologist Ian Lisk said.

El Niño - or the warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean - is continuing to strengthen and is expected peak in November or December as a historic event.

However, it is just one of several factors that could affect the UK's weather.

"While this event may become one of the strongest El Niño events on record, that does not automatically mean more severe impacts for the UK," he added.

A wetter outlook for late autumn and into winter will bring some relief to parched regions for the UK.

While the weather has recently turned more unsettled, there has so far been no change to the drought status, according to the Environment Agency (EA) National Drought Group, which met on Thursday.

Helen Wakeham, Director of Water at the EA said "drought recovery is a very long process" and only over once reservoirs, rivers and groundwater supplies are back to normal.

While the rainfall will be welcome, it is possible the UK could experience another round of "weather whiplash" where the pattern moves from one extreme to another.

A similar scenario played out in 2025 when the UK experienced a summer of record-breaking heat followed by storms and floods in the autumn.

Autumn is also likely to be warmer than normal, according to the Met Office.

It comes after summer 2026 was provisionally declared the hottest on record , following five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).

While a warmer-than-normal autumn is is consistent with global warming trends, the higher-than-normal sea surface temperatures around the UK will also have an influence.

The series of extreme heatwaves since late spring resulted in marine heatwaves , where sea surface temperatures have risen up to 5C above normal.

Warmer seas around the UK tend to keep land temperatures higher than they would otherwise normally be.

While it is unlikely the UK will see any snowfall this autumn, it is still too early to say if the winter will be especially cold or snowy.

El Niño years do bring an enhanced chance of cold and snowy weather in late winter across north-west Europe. However, the UK's position on the edge of the Atlantic complicates this.

Other meteorological influences can prevent the northerly or easterly winds that bring colder air.

Looking back at previous winters that followed a strong El Niño since 1900, just one - the winter of 1982/83 - saw widespread disruptive snow.

articles.title: Former hockey players at University of Michigan sue, say they were sexually abused decades ago
articles.summary: More than a dozen former hockey players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging their coach and other staff were aware of sexual hazing that included the forced shaving of their genitals and other abuse by teammates decades ago.
articles.body: DETROIT — More than a dozen former hockey players are suing the University of Michigan, alleging their coach and other staff were aware of sexual hazing that included the forced shaving of their genitals and other abuse by teammates decades ago. “The abuse was ritualized, meticulously planned, and sadistic. ... Enduring sexual abuse was required to be a member of the Michigan Men’s Ice Hockey team,” attorney Michael Pitt said in a sex discrimination lawsuit filed Wednesday in federal court in Detroit. The plaintiffs are 16 men who played at Michigan between 1984 and 2001. The lawsuit apparently grew out of conversations among several former teammates in 2024. The university said the allegations are “disturbing,” but denies responsibility. “To the extent any former student athlete engaged in hazing or other misconduct, they were violating university policy,” spokesperson Paul Corliss said in a written statement. “The university first adopted an official anti-hazing policy in 1982. It was one of the first universities in the country to do so, and it has earned its standing as a leader in this area,” he said. The 72-page document describes players being forced to consume excessive amounts of alcohol and eat live fish. A common allegation: They were forced to have hair around their genitals shaved by teammates. A player identified as John Doe 7 said he was taunted with a blowtorch while on a table. The lawsuit says Red Berenson, who was coach from 1984 to 2017, was aware of the abuse and did not intervene. John Doe 3 said he told Berenson that he didn’t want to participate in the hazing. The coach coerced him by telling him to be a “Michigan Man” and a ”good teammate,” according to the lawsuit. Berenson, 86, declined to comment when reached by The Associated Press. He told MLive.com there was a “certain element of initiation” by the team’s seniors, but no one had complained to him. “Were there some mishaps? Were there some bad experiences? Possibly, but it wasn’t a matter of direction or encouragement from the coaching staff or from the administration,” Berenson, a former NHL player, said. “When they say sexual, I’m guessing they’re stretching this,” he said. Berenson announced the end of “freshman hazing” in 2012, mostly referring to first-year players being forced to carry equipment and eat team meals last. He made no mention of physical abuse but acknowledged “captains that got too carried away,” according to news reports at the time. The university could argue that the hockey players waited too long to file a lawsuit, a position it took in 2020 when former athletes sued over sexual misconduct committed decades earlier by a campus sports doctor. The university ultimately agreed to pay $490 million to settle claims by more than 1,000 people.

articles.title: California enacts new curbs on social media for children
articles.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviorally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law on Thursday new tech company restrictions barring children under 16 from exposure to behaviorally addictive features on social media platforms and banning toys containing AI companion chatbots. The two measures were among 13 bills Newsom enacted as a package designed to safeguard young people from technology seen as putting them at risk, including greater online privacy protection for minors. Another measure expanded the scope of criminal sanctions against child sexual abuse material to include any digitally altered or AI-generated content that depicts a person under the age of 18 engaged in sexual conduct. A separate measure bans, for the next four years, the manufacture and sale of toys that incorporate a companion chatbot. A related measure requires parental controls on chatbot programs, along with other safety and risk assessments. Newsom touted those regulations as the most far-reaching of their kind in the nation. The bill was dubbed “Adam’s Law,” in memory of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old boy who took his own life in April 2025 after he acted, according to his parents, on suicidal thoughts validated in months of discussion with OpenAI’s ChatGPT program. OpenAI has said it intends to improve ChatGPT safeguards, which the company has acknowledged became “less reliable” as user interactions grow more prolonged. “We want our children — and every California kid — to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom, a Democrat, said in a statement announcing the measures. California, home of such leading internet companies as Google, Meta Platforms and Snap Inc, joins a growing list of U.S. states cracking down on business strategies seen as deliberately designed to hook teenagers on social media, despite evidence that extensive use is harmful to their mental health. While gaining broad bipartisan support, some critics objected to the bill as an unnecessary restriction on young people’s internet access, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the bill “a massive privacy and free speech nightmare.” Utah became the first to adopt laws regulating children’s access to social media, followed by others, including Arkansas, Louisiana, Ohio, Texas, Florida and New York, though approaches have varied. ‘Psychologically exploitative’ features targeted Countries around the world have also moved to curb children’s access to harmful internet content, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16. California‘s version, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits children under age 16 from exposure to a number of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.” Those include infinite-scroll feeds, algorithmic autoplay and other features to be defined in future regulations. Its enactment comes at a time when Big Tech, in the face of mounting legal challenges, has shown greater willingness to accept new restrictions. Meta agreed three weeks ago to pay as much as $18 billion over the next decade and strictly limit how teenagers use its Facebook and Instagram platforms under a deal with nearly all U.S. states to resolve civil claims that the company designed its social media platforms to addict children.

articles.title: ‘I want to cry’: Afghan medical students in Pakistan face expulsion fear
articles.summary: A court has temporarily suspended a directive to expel the students, but the threat of eviction lingers.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Alishba*, a medical student, was on a maternity ward night shift in Lahore when her phone began filling with messages on September 8.

“Someone said, ‘We’ve received a notification that almost 20 students are being expelled,’” she told Al Jazeera. “My first reaction was, this is nonsense. How could a government expel students from universities without any reason?”

By morning, it was not nonsense. She was one of nearly two dozen Afghan nationals named on her college’s expulsion list, circulating on Facebook within hours, all given less than three days to prepare to leave the only country where, as a woman, she has been able to study medicine at all.

On September 1, the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC), the country’s medical regulator, ordered universities and colleges to send enrolled Afghan students home. They were also barred from any new admissions, transfers or migrations of Afghan nationals for the current academic year.

In all, more than 200 Afghan students are currently enrolled in Pakistani medical or dental colleges, according to the PMDC, and most of them have been hit.

On September 11, they got temporary reprieve: Lahore High Court on Friday suspended the implementation of the PMDC directives, hearing petitions from Afghan students. The petitioners, represented by advocate Asad Jamal, argued PMDC had exceeded its jurisdiction under its own governing act and that students had been “condemned unheard”, their rights to education, life and dignity violated without any opportunity to respond.

The court noted some petitioners had studied in Pakistan for four years before now being told to leave. “Until yesterday, these were favoured children,” Justice Khalid Ishaq remarked. “Today, the policy has changed.”

The case returns to court on September 18, by which point PMDC, the Ministry of National Health Services, and the vice chancellors of affected institutions are required to file their responses. Until then, the students have respite from any punitive measure, Jamal, their lawyer, said.

“The judge very clearly stated in the courtroom that the students will be allowed to sit their exams, join classes, resume studies, and go back to their hostels, and no coercive measures can be taken against them,” he told Al Jazeera.

But the threat of expulsion lingers – a fear students must now live with, alongside their studies, while the case proceeds in court.

“I want to cry every minute,” Alishba said. “We are not dolls for them to play with. This is our life.”

In a statement issued to justify its directive, the PMDC had argued that all foreign students enrolled in Pakistani medical or dental institutions needed to be registered with the regulator.

It said “only 22 are presently registered” with the PMDC – including 14 who have graduated, and eight who are about to graduate.

But many of the other students came through the Allama Iqbal Scholarship, a programme run by Pakistan’s Higher Education Commission (HEC) with the Pakistani embassy in Kabul for top-scoring Afghan students.

And the students say neither any Pakistani government agency nor their colleges told them at the time that they also needed to register with the PMDC, a body that – per its official mandate – both oversees medical practitioners and is supposed to register medical and dental students.

“I came to Pakistan in 2021,” Alishba said. “They [Pakistan] provided us the scholarship, processed entirely through HEC and the embassy.”

Nevertheless, within days of the PMDC directive, institutions across different parts of the country began issuing eviction notices, in some cases giving students as little as 24 hours to clear their hostel rooms.

The order comes amid a broader, years-long expulsion drive that has coincided with a dramatic plunge in relations between Islamabad and the Taliban government in Kabul, marked by a rise in cross-border attacks and clashes along the two countries’ shared border.

Pakistan launched what it called the Illegal Foreigners’ Repatriation Plan in late 2023 , initially targeting undocumented migrants, after authorities said Afghan nationals had carried out 14 of 24 suicide bombings recorded in the country that year.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in June this year that more than 2.4 million Afghan nationals had returned since the drive began, describing it, in a message marking World Refugee Day, as a “phased, orderly and dignified repatriation process”.

But to the medical and dental students now being forced to leave their studies midway, there’s nothing orderly or dignified about the way they are being treated.

For Zainab*, a final-year student at another Lahore medical college, the order is the second time a change of government has closed a medical school door to her.

She had completed one semester at Kabul University of Medical Sciences when the Taliban seized power in August 2021, ending her studies there, as part of the group’s broader ban on women in higher education.

She later won her place in Pakistan through the HEC scholarship.

In her second year in Lahore, Zainab said, she walked into her college’s student affairs office and asked a simple question: Was she registered with PMDC?

She was told not to worry about it, that registration would come later, after graduation. Three years on, that unanswered question has become the official justification for sending her home mid-degree.

“If PMDC registration was genuinely the issue here, why wasn’t that stated anywhere?” she asked. “Why weren’t we told we weren’t registered? Why wasn’t it raised on the very first day we arrived, if it mattered this much?”

She initially held out hope the notice would not apply to her.

“But then our own university issued the same notice, and our vice chancellor called us in and told us clearly: This is a PMDC order, there is nothing we can do, come and collect your NOCs,” she said, referring to the no-objection certificates required to leave.

She has not formally been handed one. But she has been barred from lectures and hospital shifts since the notice arrived, which she says amounts to expulsion in practice, if not yet on paper.

Students interviewed by Al Jazeera describe a registration process they say was never in their own hands.

Rizwan*, a final-year medical student in Rawalpindi, said universities, not students, submit registration data to PMDC, typically once a student reaches second or third year.

“We are registered with the university, UHS and HEC,” he said, referring to the University of Health Sciences Lahore, which oversees several affected colleges. “But we are not registered with PMDC. Our registration is pending due to PMDC not approving it.”

Rizwan said the gap traces back to a regulatory upheaval that predates the current dispute.

Pakistan’s medical regulator was dissolved in 2019 under a presidential ordinance and replaced by a newly created body called the Pakistan Medical Commission (PMC).

In 2022, the Islamabad High Court restored the PMDC and declared the PMC’s formation illegal, a reversal that left a backlog of students and graduates from that period without a clear registration status. PMDC has since worked through the backlog in phases for various categories of students.

Afghan students admitted during the transition, Rizwan said, were among those still waiting.

The PMDC’s directive bars institutions from facilitating any transfer or migration for Afghan students, a clause he says would strip him of even the option of continuing elsewhere.

“What if we want to continue somewhere else?” Rizwan, who is five months from finishing his degree, asked.

Students interviewed by Al Jazeera were emphatic that they had never intended to remain in Pakistan beyond their studies, and had no legal path to do so regardless.

“After graduation we are not given a visa, because our visa is extended on our student status,” Rizwan said. “When that status ends, we always go back. We can’t stay here without a visa.”

Zainab made a similar point more pointedly, rejecting any comparison with the undocumented migrants targeted by Pakistan’s wider repatriation drive.

“We are not immigrants,” she said. “We were legally invited here, legally granted a scholarship by this country, legally issued a visa every single year. This should not be happening to us.”

The picture is not uniform across the country.

Batool*, a final-year medical student in Peshawar, said her college had not issued an eviction notice so far. She said her Pakistani classmates had been unfailingly supportive.

“The culture, the language, even the food, feels remarkably close to home,” she said. “I’ve never experienced or heard anything negative from people here, not now, and not before any of this.”

Afghanistan’s Taliban government has called the decision “inhumane”. Chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the country’s Ministry of Higher Education stood ready to help returning students continue their studies.

Rights group Human Rights Watch (HRW), too, condemned the government’s decision.

“The Pakistan government’s order is shockingly short-sighted and cruel, and seems yet again aimed only at punishing Afghans because of Pakistan’s conflict with the Taliban,” Patricia Gossman, HRW’s senior associate Asia director, told Al Jazeera.

“The end result of this incredibly callous approach is to deprive Afghans of trained doctors and other medical professionals, especially women, just as the country is in the throes of a humanitarian crisis,” she added.

Two former Pakistani ambassadors to Afghanistan have also questioned the decision, urging the government to reverse it.

Mansoor Ahmad Khan urged PMDC to “reconsider its decision on Afghan students in medical colleges and universities on humanitarian grounds”, proposing students be allowed to finish their degrees before any return is arranged.

Asif Durrani, a former special representative for Afghanistan, called the expulsion “shocking”.

“Expelling these students, particularly young women who have fought against extraordinary odds simply to study, is not just an administrative matter,” Durrani wrote on X. “It is a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan’s own moral responsibility. Let them study. Let them become doctors. Let them serve their people. Reverse the decision. Give these students a future.”

Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told Al Jazeera that students holding a valid visa and registered in a degree programme “are supposed to stay in the country” and finish their studies. But he did not explain the gap between that assurance and what students describe happening on campuses.

Khan also outlined this position in response to a question from a reporter at a weekly briefing on Thursday.

HEC did not respond to questions from Al Jazeera. PMDC also did not address questions, referring Al Jazeera instead to its public statement.

Siddiq Shariati, president of the Afghan Student Union at the International Islamic University Islamabad, said the policy risked damage beyond the students immediately affected, and that he feared for his own position too, despite studying international relations rather than medicine.

“Given that PMDC has already issued a notice for all medical students, it’s entirely possible HEC could issue a similar notification next, one that applies to all Afghan students across all disciplines,” he told Al Jazeera. “If that happens, we would be forced to leave as well.”

In all, about 7,000 Afghan students are studying in Pakistani colleges, with more than 4,500 of them on Pakistan government-sponsored scholarships.

Batool, the student in Peshawar, said the consequences of any expulsion would not fall equally on male and female students.

Male students, she said, could still be admitted to universities inside Afghanistan.

“Female students are in a genuinely devastating position, because no one is going to open universities just to accommodate 200 or 300 girls trying to finish a degree,” she said. “And if they did make that exception, they’d be forced to open education more broadly to everyone, not just us, not just medicine, because the double standard would draw immediate criticism, both from inside and outside Afghanistan.”

At Alishba’s college in Lahore, the vice chancellor gave students 24 hours to vacate the hostel, warning that anyone who stayed would be reported to the authorities.

She has not yet been forced out, but has not been allowed back into class either.

“The administration has said no Afghan student is permitted in class, and our attendance won’t be counted since we’re considered expelled,” she said.

She has packed an “emergency” bag, just documents and a change of clothes, in case she is made to leave without warning.

“My mother always dreamed of seeing me in scrubs, serving female patients who have no doctors in Afghanistan,” she said. “She has already made my graduation dress. Now, all of that has faded. There is no graduation. There is no degree.

“I feel like a doll being played with between the political issues of two countries,” Alishba added. “I’ve done nothing wrong. If you brought us here and gave us seats, let us finish our degrees.”

*Names have been changed to protect the identities of the students.

articles.title: How 9/11 helped Israel sell its war on Palestinians to America
articles.summary: The ‘war on terror’ made Israeli repression easier to present as part of a shared struggle against a common enemy.
articles.body:
For me, the New York City skyline was close to home. Quite literally. I grew up just across the Hudson River, with the famed skyline of America’s biggest city visible from my bedroom window. Being a Palestinian American living just outside of the world’s most famous city meant that I spent part of my summers as a tour guide for family visiting us from the Middle East, who, like so many people around the world, wanted to see the Big Apple that the movies and live broadcasts from Times Square on New Year’s Eve had made so famous.

I took visitors to the Statue of Liberty, the Empire State Building, Central Park and the World Trade Center. My last tour was in the final days of August 2001. We went to the observation deck of the World Trade Center known as “Top of the World”. Little did I know that two weeks later that deck, where we had stood looking out at the amazing metropolis below, would come crashing down along with the entire World Trade Center, killing thousands and instantly changing the world as we had known it.

By the time of the September 11 attacks, I was back in my dormitory at university in New England and huddled around a 10-inch television screen with floormates watching ABC’s Peter Jennings cover the horrific news as it was unfolding that Tuesday morning. Among the early reactions was one from Benjamin Netanyahu, then a former prime minister of Israel. Asked by The New York Times what the attack meant for relations between the United States and Israel, Netanyahu replied, “It’s very good.” Then he edited himself: “Well, not very good, but it will generate immediate sympathy,” adding that the attack would “strengthen the bond between our two peoples”. This was his response while ground zero was still smouldering after an attack that had killed nearly 3,000 people.

It immediately hit me that not only was the world about to change, but my life in the US as a Palestinian American was about to become far, far more complicated. The US was about to embark on military engagement in the Middle East, and Netanyahu was excited by the opportunity this presented Israel.

To better understand the impact this moment had on US-Israel relations, it is crucial to consider the preceding context. I have argued elsewhere that the period between the end of the Cold War and 9/11 was a complicated one for US-Israel relations. For most of the history of the US-Israel relationship, the Cold War was the defining paradigm in international relations. For Israel, this was an easy paradigm to navigate. It billed itself to Americans as a like-minded, US-aligned democracy confronting Soviet-backed satellite states in the Arab world.

But as the Cold War ended, the political landscape shifted. The Berlin Wall fell, democratisation swept Eastern Europe, and apartheid ended in South Africa, while Israel was brutally repressing the first Palestinian Intifada. Suddenly, Israel did not fit so comfortably in this new world order. It was during this period that the US made its greatest investments in Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking, however flawed, and used some leverage to press the Israeli government on settlement building.

September 11 and the ensuing global “war on terror” changed all of this. With the second Palestinian Intifada under way, the September 11 attacks on the US provided an opportunity to once again put Israel and the US on the same side of a new defining global divide. Instead of communism, the new global bad guy was radical Islam.

Netanyahu and his allies understood this very well, just as he made clear to The New York Times 25 years ago this week. A wounded America was primed for Islamophobic narratives, and pro-Israel voices were often happy to provide them, as they understood that an America obsessed with “counterterrorism” would have to stay close to Israel.

There are numerous areas where we see the impact of this over time: enhanced US-Israel intelligence collaboration, growing US financial support for Israel and legislative initiatives supported by Israel’s backers in the US that used broadened anti-terror authorities to crack down on Palestinians, to name a few.

The narratives that helped support these outcomes also went beyond simply linking Israel and the US through a common “terrorist threat”. Palestinians were also more easily turned into a “security problem” to American audiences. Instead of asking why Palestinians were resisting oppression, American audiences were pushed to see Israeli repression as self-defence similar to US behaviour. Muslims were often cast as one of two types in American discourse: moderate or extremist, and those criticising Israel were routinely placed in the latter category, which led to stigma and a chilling effect.

Israeli military practices could be cast as useful for America as well. Surveillance, counterinsurgency, targeted killings and other tactics Israel had used in the West Bank and Gaza, which had occasionally been criticised by Washington, were used by American forces in Iraq and Afghanistan and thus increasingly legitimised before American audiences.

Some of the greatest purveyors of the Islamophobic narratives that characterised much of the post-9/11 period in the United States included David Horowitz, who consistently sought to connect Palestinians with terrorism and called for profiling to make Palestinian identity itself a security concern; Daniel Pipes, who often characterised Muslim organisations as potentially or secretly militant, casting suspicion on Muslim advocacy; Steven Emerson, who sought to popularise infiltration narratives to try to turn mainstream Muslim organisations into security subjects; Brigitte Gabriel, who regularly framed Islamism as a civilisational threat, thus casting Israel as a front-line defender of the West; and David Yerushalmi, who sought to expand the threat narrative to Sharia law and Muslim political influence, thus casting Muslim political participation as potentially subversive.

The general logic of these narratives was that terrorism was effectively synonymous with all things Palestinian/Arab/Muslim and thus Israel’s security model should be seen as legitimate, if not ideal, by Americans.

It is important 25 years later to reflect on the dangerous political opportunism that spewed hate into American discourse to cast Israel and Israeli policy in a favourable light. A quarter-century later, the US is once again embroiled in a seemingly intractable quagmire, this time in Iran, a losing effort that has already cost Americans more than $100bn through higher petrol and diesel prices. Given all of this, Americans today should be quick to question Islamophobic narratives, the dangerous paths they lead down and the real motives of those who spread them.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine student suspended by King’s College London returns to campus
articles.summary: College lifts suspension amid criticism from student groups over crackdown on pro-Palestine sentiments.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – A 22-year-old Egyptian student suspended from King’s College London (KCL) last year after his involvement in pro-Palestine campus activism is returning to university.

KCL lifted Usama Ghanem’s suspension late last month, allowing him to return and complete the third and final year of his international studies degree.

“We won,” Ghanem said. “I was suspended because of my activism for Palestine … The injustices and the process that I’ve gone through have felt extremely bitter, but it also needed to be fought.”

According to a May 2025 letter addressed to Ghanem and seen by Al Jazeera, KCL accused him of several instances of non-academic misconduct, including “acting in an intimidating and hostile manner”, disrupting an event, “procedural breaches” and “causing a health and safety concern”.

The letter signed by university staff also stated: “You will need to return to your home country during this period of suspension.”

Ghanem’s visa was revoked as a result of the disciplinary action. But as he had previously been detained in Egypt over his activism, he had claimed that he risked persecution if he returned.

After taking legal action against the university and accepting delays to his studies, Ghanem told Al Jazeera: “I’m left with nothing but conviction, and the only regret I’ll ever have is that I didn’t do more for the Palestinian people.”

The campaign group Cage said, “This is a victory not just for Ghanem, but for every student at King’s, across London and beyond who has taken a stand for Palestine and for the right to protest.”

In July, Al Jazeera and Liberty Investigates reported that at least 26 students at KCL had faced disciplinary investigations after engaging in pro-Palestine protest activity between October 2023 and November 2025.

Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, several universities across the UK have faced criticism over their handling of Palestine solidarity protests on campus.

Earlier this year, the European Legal Support Center documented what it described as widespread repression of students, academics and teachers over their solidarity with Palestine, identifying educational institutions among those leading the crackdown.

KCL denies disciplining students for activism.

A university spokesperson told Al Jazeera that KCL had “upheld the original reasons” for Ghanem’s suspension but had determined that he “had met the conditions agreed for suspension and that re-enrolment was therefore the appropriate outcome”.

“We will always apply a fair approach to misconduct proceedings, and have a duty to act where behaviour breaches safeguarding and security regulations, or puts others at risk,” the spokesperson said.

They added that decisions on visa sponsorship are not made by KCL, but that the university “has a legal duty to notify (UK Visas & Immigration) of any change in student status”.

Al Jazeera has also seen evidence indicating that KCL used Horus , a private firm run by former military intelligence officials, to monitor protest activity.

In Ghanem’s case, the company appeared to have informed the university of upcoming demonstrations in support of the “expelled student”.

“They have specifically been engaged in surveilling me,” Ghanem said. “I think it’s crystal clear that King’s overreached.”

KCL denied monitoring Ghanem, saying “all information collated by Horus is already publicly available elsewhere.

“We use Horus as a horizon scanning tool for updates on events on or near our campuses, including protests on any subject,” the university said.

Hundreds of students and several academics supported Ghanem throughout his dispute with KCL, including the Association of Student Activism for Palestine (ASAP).

“KCL’s decision to reinstate Usama shows what happens when students and the wider community stand strong against the intimidation tactics of our universities,” ASAP told Al Jazeera.

“This victory has shown us the power that students and the wider movement holds when we stand on the side of justice unwaveringly.”

articles.title: In 2016, US dairy farmers dumped 43 million gallons of milk, the largest recorded loss in at least 16 years, as production outran the plants able to process it
articles.summary: US News: In 2016, U.S. dairy farmers faced a catastrophic crisis, leading to more than 43 million gallons of milk being dumped due to excess production and low demand, making it the highest recorded waste in 16 years. The situation resulted from a prolonged market imbalance after 2014 price surges and weak global dairy demand, especially from China.
articles.body: In the first eight months of 2016, US dairy producers and handlers discarded, dumped, or lost more than 43 million gallons of milk. The US Department of Agriculture’s data suggest that the volume was the largest amount of milk wasted in at least 16 years of comparable information. Some of the discarded or dumped milk went into fields, manure lagoons or animal feed. Meanwhile, some was lost along truck routes or discarded at processing plants. The Wall Street Journal report said the amount was equivalent to about 66 Olympic-size swimming pools.As raw milk is perishable, it cannot be stored indefinitely while producers wait for prices or demand to improve. Concurrently, dairy processors were dealing with large inventories of products like cheese. This resulted in a bottleneck in which some milk had little practical or economic destination, driven by the unceasing daily output of herds managed on continuous, year-round calving and lactation schedules.How a 2014 price increase fed the later glutThe imbalance was no sudden change. Instead, it had been building for more than a year. In September 2014, the US all-milk price reached $25.70 per hundredweight, which is equal to 100 pounds of milk. High prices encouraged dairy farmers to expand production, and US milk output subsequently rose to 208.6 billion pounds in 2015. This was 1.2% above 2014. Market analysts explained that dairy production responds slowly to changing prices because expanding or reducing herds takes time.The production response continued even after the prices began falling. By April 2016, the all-milk price had dropped to $15 per hundredweight, which had fallen sharply from the peak in 2014. Yet in June 2016, the USDA forecasted that annual output would refuse to bend, holding steady at a projected 212.6 billion pounds. Industry tracking noted that farmers could reduce some costs or remove less productive cows. Though, many costs associated with maintaining a dairy herd could not be avoided simply by cutting production.Another reason why output remained high was that the production costs were relatively favourable. The agency’s later review of 2016 found that feed prices had fallen during late 2015 and remained low through most of 2016. Milk production per cow also increased, and by the end of the year, the country had produced a record 212.5 billion pounds of milk, 1.7% more than in 2015. The average milk production per cow rose by 1.4%.The challenge, therefore, was that production was responding with a lag to the favourable economics of the earlier period, while the international market had changed considerably. Several federal reports suggest that global demand for dairy products was relatively weak, particularly in China, while the US dollar remained strong. Several major producing countries had also redirected European dairy products toward markets where US exporters competed due to Russia’s ban on most dairy imports. In addition to that, the European Union ended its milk supply quotas in April 2015, after which EU milk production increased and added to global supplies.When the surplus reached the processing systemWhile the dairy products are traded globally, the effects eventually appeared inside the US supply chain. The government agency reported that exports of some major dairy products weakened between 2014 and 2015, while imports increased. Cheese exports fell by 114 million pounds, or 14%, and dry-whey exports declined by 106 million pounds, or 22%. At the same time, imports of cheese and butter increased, leaving milk and dairy products competing for domestic processing, storage and sales channels.On the other hand, for farmers and milk handlers, converting surplus raw milk into another dairy product was not always an immediate solution. Contemporary reporting noted that some producers could find themselves better off disposing of milk than moving it to a processor when the economics of transportation and processing stopped working. Therefore, the industry started exploring different ways to absorb milk through existing consumer markets. Dairy Management Inc. worked with food companies and restaurant chains to increase the amount of dairy ingredients used in products. Although these measures could increase demand, they were incremental responses to a much bigger imbalance in production and inventories.Why lower farm prices did not mean equally cheap milk in the marketThe collapse in farm prices was substantial, but consumers did not experience the same percentage decline at stores. USDA reported that prices received by dairy farmers fell about 40% between September 2014 and April 2016. Over approximately the same period, the retail price of whole milk fell 16%, from $3.77 per gallon in October 2014 to $3.16 in April 2016.By the end of 2016, the industry’s financial picture remained difficult despite the record production. The annual average all-milk price fell to $16.24 per hundredweight from $17.12 in 2015. While prices staged a modest late-season rally to reach an average of $17.67 per hundredweight in the fourth quarter, the annual figure still heavily reflected the impact of the earlier collapse. The government agency attributed the relatively low 2016 prices to the combination of abundant global supplies, relatively slow demand growth in some markets, continued Russian trade restrictions and stronger European competition, along with the strong US dollar.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: MIKE PENCE: Remember the fallen — and the generation that defended America since 9/11
articles.summary: From the World Trade Center to the hunt for Usama bin Laden and ISIS, a generation of Americans answered the call after the September 11 attacks.
articles.body: On September 11, 2001, shortly after the terrorists struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, I walked across the street to the Capitol, swimming against a sea of pandemonium. Later, I joined other members in the basement of the Capitol Hill Police headquarters for a briefing on what we knew — and what might happen next. Former Governor Tom Ridge, then serving as President George W. Bush’s homeland security adviser, told us, "The only thing we know for sure is that they want to hit us again, and they want to hit us worse." TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE Long before 2001, radical Islamic terrorism was at war with America’s way of life and had already established a terrible rhythm in our national life. The 1983 Beirut barracks bombing killed 241 American servicemen. Pan Am Flight 103 was blown out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, killing 270 people, including 190 Americans. The first World Trade Center bombing came in 1993: six dead, more than 1,000 injured, with the terrorists hoping to topple one tower into the other. In 1998, al Qaeda bombed our embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, killing 224 people and injuring thousands. Two years later, al Qaeda struck again, bombing the USS Cole in Yemen and killing 17 American sailors. LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11 Our government’s response had fallen into a near slumber of its own. Terrorists attacked. Americans mourned. Investigators pursued those responsible. Security was tightened and warnings were issued. Then life moved on — until the terrorists struck again. For all the courage and skill of those fighting terrorism in those years, America remained largely reactive, responding to attacks rather than preventing them and ensuring that they could never happen again. September 11 broke that rhythm forever. From the firefighters and police who rushed into the Twin Towers without regard to their personal safety, to those who charged the cockpit in the skies over Pennsylvania, America’s defenders surged forward with what felt like all new resolve to take the fight directly to our terrorist enemies. HOW 9/11 TRANSFORMED SYNAGOGUE SECURITY INTO A NEW REALITY FOR THE JEWISH COMMUNITY America resolved that we would no longer simply bring terrorists to justice after they attacked us. We would find them before they could strike, take the fight to them abroad, and build new defenses here at home. Twenty-five years later, we should remember the heroes forged that day, and we should acknowledge the generation of selfless Americans who have delivered on that promise every day since. In the aftermath of the attacks, young men and women lined up around the block outside military recruiting offices determined to serve our country. Nearly 3 million American servicemen and women deployed in the wars that followed September 11. More than 7,000 gave their lives and tens of thousands were wounded. They destroyed terrorist sanctuaries, hunted down al Qaeda leaders and brought Usama bin Laden to justice. When ISIS later established a terrorist caliphate across vast stretches of Iraq and Syria, American forces and our allies destroyed it, liberating nearly 110,000 square kilometers of territory and freeing 7.7 million people from its brutal rule. But, America’s defenders are not found only on distant battlefields. Some chose careers in law enforcement, disrupting terrorist plans on the homefront and chasing leads that never made the evening news. Others joined the Border Patrol, standing watch on the ground while air marshals guarded the skies. In New York City, 58 children of FDNY firefighters who made the ultimate sacrifice on September 11 have grown up to join the same department their fathers served. Their greatest accomplishment is measured by what did not happen. The nightmare we feared that day — a succession of increasingly catastrophic terrorist attacks on the American homeland — never came to pass. NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS Not because our enemies quit trying, but because America’s defenders stopped them cold. For a generation, Americans have been able to live their lives without the constant fear that another September 11 was around the corner. That peace was earned by Americans whose names we know and countless others whose names we never will — by those who served both at home and overseas, those who came home wounded, those who never came home at all, and those who still stand watch today. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION On this solemn anniversary, let us remember the 2,977 innocent souls who perished at the hands of our terrorist enemies on September 11. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES And let us honor those who gave their lives in the long struggle that followed. Because of the heroes forged that fateful day and every day since, the American people live in freedom and security. So let us offer the thanks of a grateful nation to all who answered the call to protect and defend America these past 25 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Our founders proclaimed eternal vigilance is the price of liberty. May we never forget or fail to honor the sacrifices made by America’s defenders from that day to this. And may we never cease to be vigilant in the defense of the land we love. So help us, God. articles.title: 9/11 attacks 25 years later: Americans share their vivid memories of Sept. 11
articles.summary: From an 11-year-old watching the towers fall on a classroom TV to a doctor treating victims in a conference room, NBC News readers share their searing memories from Sept. 11, 2001.
articles.body: After the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, the oft-repeated refrain became “Never Forget.” NBC News asked followers on social media to share their memories of that day 25 years later — the things they will never forget about one of the most pivotal mornings in American history. Answers have been lightly edited for length and clarity. All times are approximate and listed as Eastern. A harrowing morning 8:50 a.m., New Jersey: My husband and I had been in the building the evening prior and now this was happening! I watched the towers tumble like dominos on TV, something I didn’t know buildings could do. Since we lived in Northeastern, N.J., we could smell the smoke and see it. Worst of all, we could smell death. — Karen Bulloch 9 a.m., Brooklyn, N.Y.: I ran into a friend at the corner coffee shop. She had just dropped off her child and was waiting for her husband to celebrate their anniversary. He was an FDNY firefighter and was just getting off of his multi-day shift when the call came in. Instead of enjoying his anniversary, Dave Fontana stayed with his brothers. He was a beautiful soul, a wonderful husband and father. I only got to know him briefly at the Music Together program we brought our children to. — Scott Groom 9 a.m., Ashtabula, Ohio: Everyone I was around, we couldn’t stop hugging each other and trying to help those of us who were taking that day harder than others. — Trent Reinke 9 a.m., Yulee, Fla.: I was an Outward Bound instructor, getting ready to go on a 30 day canoeing expedition with “troubled” teens. We were getting life jackets and paddles ready for the students to arrive when a staff member came down to the gear locker and told us that someone had just flown a plane into the WTC. Someone actually said, “like a passenger plane?” and we all kind of laughed it off because how the hell could that happen? Well, within two minutes we were all watching the news broadcast in horror. We left on the St. Mary’s River or Suwannee the next morning and didn’t see or hear from anyone for about four days. The first time we ran into a couple of fishermen, they asked if we had heard the news. They gave us a copy of that day’s newspaper. It was kind of otherworldly to be out on a river in nature for weeks without really knowing what was happening. — Tommy Taylor 9 a.m., Guilderland, N.Y.: I was 11 and had just started middle school. I remember one girl brought cupcakes in to celebrate her birthday that morning. I was in one large classroom with a retractable divider in the middle; history/English classes on one side and math/science on the other. During math, the teacher on the other side slammed open the divider and told my teacher to turn on the TV. Years after 9/11 many people claimed they watched the events of that day unfold in classrooms on TVs. It actually happened to me and my classmates; 11-year-olds watching buildings on fire, people jumping and the towers eventually falling. — Rachel Langan 9:15 a.m., Long Island, N.Y.: I remember seeing the janitors on the roof of my school looking towards the city. — Lauren DiTusta 9:30 a.m., Tacoma, Wash.: I was on a business trip to Tacoma, Washington, from Rhode Island, for a week of training. I was watching the Today show and I vividly remember seeing the first tower fall — I worked at 2 World Trade Center in the late 1980s. I had to call family and friends at home and in New York, which was almost impossible. I finally walked to the office and we collectively decided to continue with the training as no one could get home. Given that I had worked on the 102nd floor of 2 WTC, I will forever remember people jumping from those windows. I stood at those windows many times while working for Shearson Lehman and I am still pained by how desperate they must have felt. The sadness is the same 25 years later. — Pamela Rotondo 9:35 a.m., New York: After I had finished being, yes, a victim of the collapse of Tower Two, I realized there was a lot of carnage around me. I figured the best thing I could do was to get to the nearest hospital. I can suture up a knee, probably with both hands tied behind my back and blindfolded, so to speak. So I went to Beekman Hospital. I identified myself because I didn’t work there and they gave me a fourth floor conference room. I started to sew people back together again, just trying to stop the bleeding. But that day, it was so surreal. I’m standing over a patient, trying to sew them together, and I remember how difficult it was to even pass a suture through the tissue because my mind wasn’t really focused. — Dr. Gordon Huie 9:45 a.m., Potomac, Md.: I had dropped the kids off at the school in Silver Spring and was listening to the radio, and they said a plane had crashed into the north tower of the World Trade Center. Naturally, I was interested in hearing more about what was happening. I went directly home and turned on the Today Show. When the plane crashed into the Pentagon, I got back in my car and drove to pick my kids up from school. In an attempt to not cause anxiety for the students — many of whose parents worked downtown for the government or military — the administration wanted the school day to continue as normal for as long as possible. I sat in the school’s office for a few hours to allow my three children to carry on with the day. Between noon and the end of the school day, I signed my kids out of class and we drove home. During all of this happening I had been thinking that we didn’t own an American flag, so I stopped at Michael’s on Rockville Pike to see if we could buy one. When we got home we hung the flag outside of our garage. — Debbie Silverman 9:50 a.m., New York: I remember evacuating the subway at 34th Street and seeing a gaping hole in the one tower that was remaining. Everyone was trying to call someone on a cell phone or phone booth, and people had the news blasting from open cars. The only thing I could think to do was to start walking home, back to 157th and Broadway. While I was walking back, I saw people’s expressions change into sheer shock, so I turned around and saw the second tower collapse. No one knew what was going to happen next, and we just kept walking. It felt like we were in some kind of apocalyptic movie. — Dionides Vila Dealing with the aftermath 5 p.m., Armonk, N.Y.: After hours of not being able to reach my dad, getting frantic calls from family in Italy and watching my mother assume her husband was gone, we finally got word that he was able to jump in a limo and get to the Bronx. We drove to pick him up, covered in ash. — MT 7 p.m., Manhasset, N.Y.: I remember the cars that remained in the parking lots at the Plandome and Manhasset train stations were the first hint at those who would not be coming home. — Terry Sears 7 p.m., Ellington, Conn.: I had decided a few weeks earlier to start a book club, and we set the first meeting for Tuesday, Sept 11. The day came, and of course unfolded into the horror we all remember. I emailed everyone (about 20 people) and asked, “Do you still want to get together or should we postpone?” We were so distraught — all of us with school-age children who we were trying to help understand what happened. We went back and forth on going forward. In the end, 18 of us met that night, and we were so thankful we had each other to process our shock. The TV was on in the background, showing scenes of heartbreak and grief, bravery and sacrifice. I couldn’t imagine shutting it off. We were bonded, and many of us have remained close friends since then. That original book club will honor 25 years of book discussions this September, and most importantly, 25 years of supporting each other. — Ann LaPoint-Mills 10:30 p.m., Houston: I was stationed at the main headquarters for Continental Airlines as crew coordinator. The atmosphere on the entire main floor — which housed the System Operation Control Center — was heavy with sorrow. It was overwhelming to be there, as we struggled to perform our duties while the entire system lay in a state of paralysis and unsure if we would ever move on from this tragic event. — Angel Sanchez

articles.title: JOHN ONDRASIK: What 9/11 taught us about courage, unity and the price of freedom
articles.summary: The song "Tuesday" honors September 11 victims as its creator asks whether America could still unite if another 9/11-scale attack struck today.
articles.body: 9/11 occurred on a Tuesday. In October 2009, I released a song entitled "Tuesday" — a musical plea to never forget the lessons of September 11, 2001, when Islamic terrorists murdered 2,977 innocent people on American soil. Is Monday coming back/ That’s what Mondays do/ They turn and turn around/ Afraid to see it through. Welcome to Monday. 9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS Performing my song "Superman" at Paul McCartney’s Concert for New York City was one of the great honors of my life. To spend that day — and share that stage — with heroic New York City first responders and the families of those murdered was an incredibly humbling, life-changing experience. Much of the audience at Madison Square Garden consisted of firefighters, police officers, rescue workers and others who had spent the previous month sifting through the rubble and carnage of Ground Zero. The images of thousands of people singing, screaming, crying and embracing one another remain seared into my memory. For a few hours, music gave them — and all of us — a chance to release some of the pain we carried within. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES The world sang and cried with us. You may remember what happened in the aftermath of 9/11. America came together in a way we had rarely seen before and have not seen since. There was no red America and blue America. There was only red, white and blue. Americans stood shoulder to shoulder across the country with compassion, love and resolve — and with an unequivocal commitment to bring Usama bin Laden and his terrorist network to justice. The thing about memories/ They’re sure and bound to fade/ Except for the stolen souls/ Left upon her blade. Imagine standing in your neighborhood on September 12, 2001, and telling your neighbor what America might look like 25 years later. Imagine telling them that radical leftist ideologies, hostile to America, would infiltrate some of our most prestigious universities and metastasize through mainstream and social media. That members of Congress would echo propaganda promoted by terrorist organizations such as Hamas. That candidates could associate with people who openly express hatred for America — or even suggest America deserved 9/11 — and still win elections and govern American cities. DAVID MARCUS: CALLING 9/11 'INEVITABLE' IS SAME AS JUSTIFYING IT, AND IT IS DISGRACEFUL They would not have believed you, such lunacy! The aftermath of Hamas’s October 7 terrorist attack in Israel provided another warning about the moral collapse taking hold within many of our institutions. Before Israel had even buried its dead, we witnessed people in the West rationalizing, excusing and even celebrating the slaughter. It raises an uncomfortable question: If an attack on the scale of 9/11 occurred in America today, would we still respond as one people, one country? Or would we see more mob like campus encampments, ideological justifications for terrorism, and Americans blaming their own country as the "oppressor" that somehow got what it deserved. Tuesday came and went/ One September/ When will she come again? Twenty-five years after 9/11, America finds itself in another battle — this one for the soul of our nation and, more broadly, for the future of Western civilization. The threats are not identical to those we faced in 2001. But they are real. Radical Islamism remains a global threat, while antisemitism and anti-American extremism increasingly find expression across the ideological spectrum. Ideas once confined to society’s fringes now travel instantly, and with little consequence, through universities, political movements and social media. The enemy is in the building, and time is not on our side. That is why "Never Forget" cannot become merely a slogan printed on a bumper sticker or repeated once every September. It is an obligation. It is our obligation. We have a duty to teach our children what happened on September 11, 2001: about the evil fanatics who attacked us, why they attacked us, and the carnage of what unchecked extremism can produce. But "Never Forget" means something more. It means remembering the best of us. It means telling our children about the firefighters who climbed stairwells while everyone else was running down. The police officers, paramedics and ordinary citizens who ran toward collapsing infernos to save people they had never met. The passengers of Flight 93 who understood what was happening and, knowing the probable cost, fought back. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION They represent the best of humanity. Twenty-five years later, their courage should still challenge and inspire us. Their sacrifice should remind us that America is not sustained merely by institutions, elections or slogans. It survives because generation after generation chooses to defend the principles that make the country worth defending. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Memory fades. History becomes distant. Tuesdays come and go. But some Tuesdays must never be forgotten. May the memory of those we lost — and the example of the heroes of September 11, 2001 — give us the strength, courage and fortitude to fight for America every day, especially Tuesdays, for the next 250 years. Let’s Roll…

articles.title: Japan, India, Ukraine: Why some countries are uneasy about new UN map
articles.summary: The countries are not opposed to a new map per se; they’re testy about the colour shades.
articles.body:
In a historic move last week, the United Nations General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to encourage the use of new world maps which more accurately depict continents with their true sizes.

The move followed months of lobbying by the African Union, which itself adopted a new map earlier in February. A total of 164 countries voted in favour while six abstained.

The United States was the only member to oppose it. US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said before the vote that the resolution was “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”.

“Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century,” she said.

But since the resolution was approved, at least three other countries have voiced concerns about the changes: India, Ukraine and Japan.

None are explicitly opposed to adopting a new projection. However, they are raising concerns about how certain disputed territories should be depicted.

The UN endorsed a resolution promoting the Equal Earth projection of the world map, rather than the Mercator projection, which is currently widely used.

The resolution does not ban Mercator or impose a particular replacement – it merely encourages nations to adopt the Equal Earth version, which was created by three researchers in 2018.

The Mercator projection, which was produced by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 when the West was busy “conquering” new territories, attempts to show a three-dimensional globe on a two-dimensional surface. That is why countries closer to the poles appear much larger than countries at the equator.

For decades, map experts have pointed out that Mercator’s projection disproportionately shrinks the true size of the African continent and that of other developing regions, while making Europe and the US seem much larger by comparison.

For example, Greenland is shown as roughly the same size as Africa, but, in reality, it could fit into the continent 14 times over. Europe, which is portrayed as bigger than South America, is actually half its size.

Advocates from African countries pointed out that the map is problematic because of the size issues. Importantly, they argued, it reinforces negative perceptions of Africa.

Several cartographers have attempted to develop equal area maps. However, African activists specifically pushed for the Equal Earth projection map, which significantly expands Africa and shrinks Europe and the US.

Experts say while maps are inherently inaccurate because of the constraints of depicting a spherical world on a flat plane, the Equal Earth projection is as close as it gets.

Why is Ukraine worried about the new map?

Ukraine was one of six countries which abstained from the vote at the UNGA, along with Estonia, Georgia, Moldova, Serbia and Lithuania, who voted in solidarity with Ukraine.

Kyiv has complained that the Equal Earth projection depicts the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula in a distinctly lighter shade than mainland Ukraine.

Russia illegally occupied and annexed Crimea in February 2014, a move the UN has denounced.

Although the peninsula is also shaded differently from mainland Russia on the new map, its yellowish tint appears closer to the Russian shade than Ukraine’s.

“Ukraine does not in principle oppose the core issue addressed in this draft resolution,” Andrii Melnyk, the country’s permanent representative to the UN, said in an address to the assembly.

Melnyk said Kyiv had asked for corrections before the vote but had not received positive responses. The new map, he said, could be tantamount to opening a Pandora’s box, enabling the “abuse and distortion” of the world map.

“It would be a truly fatal mistake for all of us, and for this General Assembly, to seek to correct a historical injustice in the geographical depiction of countries and continents by simultaneously allowing a deeply troubling interpretation of the text of this draft resolution,” he added.

Meanwhile, on Thursday, Tokyo, which voted in favour of the new map, said it had also asked for corrections to the Equal Earth projection because the map uses the same colours and shades for Russian territory as it does for the disputed Kuril Islands.

Russia and Japan have long fought over control of the four islands, known in Russia as the Southern Kurils and in Japan as the Northern Territories. In 1945, during World War II, the Soviet Union invaded and annexed the islands as part of a pact with Western Allies that stipulated the Soviets would take the disputed territory. The islands’ Japanese inhabitants were removed.

Subsequently, Japan and the US have claimed that the islands were not part of the original pact. The islands, however, remain under Russian administration.

In August this year, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin paid his first-ever visit to the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable”, saying it “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”.

This week, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the Japanese embassy in the US has asked Equal Earth’s creators to change the map.

“Displays that contradict the Japanese government’s position are seen [on the map],” Kihara said at a news conference. “We need to prevent incorrect perceptions regarding our country’s territories and geographical names from spreading.”

India also voted in favour of the Equal Earth projection, but on Sunday, the Ministry of External Affairs published a caveat regarding depictions of the disputed border territory of Kashmir.

Following the Indian partition of 1947, both Pakistan and India lay claim to the former state of Jammu and Kashmir, which had been controlled by the British through indirect rule. The region has subsequently been a flashpoint for tensions between the two rivals and has led to several wars.

Parts of Kashmir are administered by Pakistan, while other parts are administered by India. China, which also disputes some Kashmir territory with India, administers its northeastern portion.

In his statement, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal noted that the UN vote was in favour of encouraging the use of equal area projections and that it had not made the use of any one map mandatory.

“India’s sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India’s official map,” he said. “Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable.”

articles.title: Bristol city centre artwork to be repainted in summer of 2027
articles.summary: The giant colourful artwork will be repainted next summer with more durable paint.
articles.body:
The large fading piece of artwork in Bristol City Centre is due to be repainted next summer with a more durable material.

The "Our Common Ground" artwork was painted on the floor where the fountains were in September last year but quickly began to fade away .

It was painted with a water-based road line marking paint. Bristol City Council has now decided to use thermoplastics, which was initially discounted as too expensive.

The total budget for the artwork was £61,000, half of which came from the city council.

Liberal Democrat Councillor Andrew Brown, chair of the economy and skills policy committee, said thermoplastic paint would be more reliable.

Thermoplastics are often used for road markings such as white lane dividers and zebra crossings, and can last for several years without needing maintenance.

Brown said: "Research into alternative solutions has been conducted after the initial painted solution was unsuccessful.

"This has identified thermoplastics as a more durable and reliable treatment."

He added the project was "inherited from the previous administration".

The first phase of the revamp will involve cleaning, surface treatment, and testing a small area.

This test phase will apply a thermoplastic solution instead of paint in September or October. It will be left over winter to establish how during it is through the colder and wetter weather.

If the test is successful, the second phase will involve the reinstatement of the full artwork in spring or summer next year, said the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

The council originally commissioned Upfest and the artist Oshii to coordinate the painting of the mural. However, it is understood Upfest is no longer involved in the project.

articles.title: Dating to 1898, Nipomo's oldest church served the California town for over a century; 128 years later, its owners donated it to become a museum, event venue and visitor center
articles.summary: US News: Dating back to 1898, Nipomo’s oldest church has been part of the California town’s community life for more than a century. Now, 128 years after it fir.
articles.body: Dating back to 1898, Nipomo’s oldest church has been part of the California town’s community life for more than a century. Now, 128 years after it first opened, the historic building has been donated to the Dana Adobe and Cultural Center, which plans to turn it into a community hub with a museum, event space and visitor centre.The church stands at the intersection of Tefft Street and Thompson Road, across from Jocko’s Steakhouse, News Channel 3-12 reported. John and Rebecca Prewett, who bought the building in 2015, recently donated it to the local non-profit organisation.The Dana Adobe and Cultural Center runs the nearby historic Dana Adobe, described as Nipomo’s oldest settlement and dating to 1839. With the church now under its ownership, the organisation wants to use the building to connect residents and visitors with the area’s history while giving the community a new space.Jim Corridan, president of the Dana Adobe and Cultural Center, said the building was originally Saint Joseph’s Church. It served as Nipomo’s first church and remained the main church until the 1970s, when a new Saint Joseph’s Church was built."Last week the Adobe received the church," Corridan said. "It was the original Saint Joseph's Church and began in 1898. It was used as the first church and the main church until the 1970s when a new Saint Joseph's Church was built. Since then, it's gone through a number of different things, but most recently it's been the Cavalry Church."Church to continue Sunday servicesThe building will retain its current religious use even as the new plans take shape. Corridan said Calvary Church will remain there and continue holding its weekly Sunday morning services.Alongside that, the Dana Adobe and Cultural Center plans to give the building several new community uses. The organisation wants the church to strengthen the Dana Adobe’s presence in downtown Nipomo and become part of the Old Towne community."One of the biggest goals for Dana is to help make a presence for the Adobe here in downtown," Corridan said. "We also want to make this part of the center of Old Towne and the community of Nipomo so that people can utilize the space, reconnect to the history of the community and have a better understanding of the region, and so we're really excited to be able to offer this kind of as a mini community center for the citizens of Nipomo and especially here in Old Towne."Historic building planned as 'Visit Nipomo' centreAnother key part of the plan is to create a "Visit Nipomo" centre in the building. The centre will provide tourists with information about Nipomo and the South County region.Visitors will be able to use the space to find out what is happening in the area and get information on where to eat, stay, visit and shop."We have some new ideas," Corridan said. "We're going to be making this a historical museum, a portion of it. We're also going to be making a venue here so that we can have people use the side yard and the church for different events, and perhaps most importantly, is that we're going to make this a 'Visit Nipomo' center.""It will be a place where tourists can stop and find out what's going on in Nipomo and in the South County region, but also utilize it as a way point to figure out where to eat, where to stay, where to visit, and where to shop in this region," he added.Repairs planned for 128-year-old churchThe Dana Adobe and Cultural Center also plans to carry out repairs and improvements to the building over time, depending on contributions and donations. Corridan said the organisation plans to repaint the church and explore adding stained glass or stained glass film to recreate the appearance of the former windows.It also hopes to backlight the windows so that the original windows can be seen from the intersection of Thompson and Tefft."One of our big goals is over time, as contributions and donations come in, to preserve this building and fix little things that are needing repair," Corridan said. "We'll repaint it and hopefully put in some version of stained glass or stained glass film to replicate the stained glass that used to be in the church, so that it shines like it did before, and with luck, we'll end up back lighting all the windows so that when you drive down this corner at Thompson and Tefft, you'll see the stunning views of the original windows."Corridan hopes the work and planned additions will be completed sometime next year.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
